title: Conjecture 1.1 (Erdős-Hajnal conjecture for tournaments)
statement_text: For every tournament $H$ there exists $\tau > 0$ such that every $H$-free tournament $G$ has a transitive subtournament with at least $|G|^{\tau}$ vertices.
context_text: The Erdős-Hajnal conjecture was raised as a question by Erdős and Hajnal and asserts that for every graph $H$ there exists $\tau > 0$ such that every graph $G$ not containing an induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$ has a clique or stable set of cardinality at least $|G|^{\tau}$. Alon, Pach and Solymosi showed this is equivalent to the stated tournament formulation. A tournament satisfying 1.1 is said to have the EH-property (or weak EH-property).
paper_contribution: Proves the strong EH-property (which implies the EH-property) for every tournament with at most six vertices, except possibly $P_7^-$, $H_6$, and $\overline{H_6}$, extending the result of Berger, Choromanski and Chudnovsky who showed every tournament on at most six vertices has the EH-property except possibly $P_7^-$.
notes: The exponent in the PDF reads as |G|τ (PDF garble); context makes clear this is |G|^{\tau}.
paper_title: Pure pairs. X. Tournaments and the strong Erdos-Hajnal property

title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: A tournament has the strong EH-property if and only if it admits a numbering for which the backedge graph is a forest.
context_text: Tournaments are finite; a tournament $G$ is $H$-free if it has no subtournament isomorphic to $H$. A pure pair in a tournament $G$ is an ordered pair $(A,B)$ of disjoint vertex sets such that every vertex of $B$ is adjacent from every vertex of $A$ (all edges go from $A$ to $B$); its order is $\min(|A|,|B|)$. A tournament $H$ has the strong EH-property if there is $c>0$ such that every $H$-free tournament $G$ with $|G|>1$ has a pure pair of order at least $c|G|$; this implies the (weak) EH-property, that some $\tau>0$ makes every $H$-free tournament $G$ contain a transitive subtournament on $|G|^\tau$ vertices (the tournament Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asserts that all tournaments have it). For a numbering $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $H$, the backedge graph is the ordered graph on $V(H)$ in which, for $i<j$, $v_iv_j$ is an edge (a backedge) iff the edge of $H$ is directed from $v_j$ to $v_i$. $D_5$ is the unique $5$-vertex tournament in which every vertex has out-degree two. For graphs, the authors previously proved that a graph $H$ has the analogous strong property (linear pure pairs in graphs excluding $H$ and $\overline{H}$ as induced subgraphs) if and only if $H$ or $\overline{H}$ is a forest. For tournaments they prove one direction: every tournament with the strong EH-property admits a numbering whose backedge graph is a forest. They initially found the converse unlikely, but tried hard to disprove it and failed, and pose it as a conjecture. They are far from proving it: the tournament $P_7^-$ has a backedge graph that is a forest with four edges, yet they cannot even show it has the weak EH-property. They prove that tournaments with a numbering with at most three backedges have the strong EH-property (except one undecided case), so every tournament with at most six vertices has it except three undecided ones, and give a seven-vertex tournament $P_7$ without it.
paper_title: Pure pairs. X. Tournaments and the strong Erdos-Hajnal property

title: Informal question: can the D5-freeness hypothesis in Theorem 1.6 be dropped?
statement_text: Let $H$ be a tournament that admits a numbering $(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ for which the backedge graph $B$ has at most three edges. The authors prove that if moreover $H$ is $D_5$-free (that is, there do not exist $1\le a<b<c<d<e\le n$ with $E(B)=\{v_av_d,v_av_e,v_bv_e\}$), then $H$ has the strong EH-property. Perhaps the $D_5$-freeness condition can be omitted, but that remains open.
context_text: Tournaments are finite; a tournament $G$ is $H$-free if it has no subtournament isomorphic to $H$. A pure pair in a tournament $G$ is an ordered pair $(A,B)$ of disjoint vertex sets such that every vertex of $B$ is adjacent from every vertex of $A$ (all edges go from $A$ to $B$); its order is $\min(|A|,|B|)$. A tournament $H$ has the strong EH-property if there is $c>0$ such that every $H$-free tournament $G$ with $|G|>1$ has a pure pair of order at least $c|G|$; this implies the (weak) EH-property, that some $\tau>0$ makes every $H$-free tournament $G$ contain a transitive subtournament on $|G|^\tau$ vertices (the tournament Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asserts that all tournaments have it). For a numbering $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $H$, the backedge graph is the ordered graph on $V(H)$ in which, for $i<j$, $v_iv_j$ is an edge (a backedge) iff the edge of $H$ is directed from $v_j$ to $v_i$. $D_5$ is the unique $5$-vertex tournament in which every vertex has out-degree two. The two forms of the $D_5$ condition are equivalent since, up to isomorphism, $D_5$ has only one backedge graph with three edges, and $D_5$ itself has the strong EH-property (Berger, Choromanski, Chudnovsky and Zerbib). The open case is thus a tournament with three backedges that contains $D_5$, i.e. whose backedge graph is $\{v_av_d,v_av_e,v_bv_e\}$ for some $a<b<c<d<e$. Every tournament with the strong EH-property admits a numbering whose backedge graph is a forest, and the authors conjecture the converse; the three-backedge theorem is a small step in this direction.
paper_title: Pure pairs. X. Tournaments and the strong Erdos-Hajnal property
